keyVerseText: And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed. Noah: Gr. Noe: that is Rest, or, Comfort
rootMeaning: The name נֹחַ (Nôach) derives from the root נוּחַ (nûwach), which means 'rest' or 'resting place.' This etymology highlights a foundational concept of quietness and relief, suggesting a place or state of cessation from toil or struggle. Beyond the English name 'Noah,' which is often seen simply as a proper noun, the root sense emphasizes a profound spiritual and physical reprieve.
usageInScripture: The word נֹחַ appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly as the proper name 'Noah,' referring to the patriarch known for building the ark and preserving humanity. Its top translations consistently identify the figure of Noah, with variations such as 'And Noah,' 'of Noah,' and 'unto Noah' showing its narrative and genealogical significance. This consistent use underscores the centrality of Noah as a symbol of deliverance and continuity in the biblical text.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding נֹחַ as 'rest' enriches the theological portrait of Noah, not merely as a historical figure but as one embodying God's provision of peace amid judgment. Noah's role as the ark-builder who preserved life through the flood mirrors God's promise of ultimate rest and restoration. This connection points forward to the Christian hope in Christ, who offers true and lasting rest from sin's toil and curse. Thus, Noah's name reminds believers of God's faithfulness to bring comfort and renewal through His covenantal work.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 5:29 states, 'And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.' Here, the name נֹחַ explicitly links to the idea of comfort and rest, highlighting that Noah represents relief from the hardships caused by the curse on the ground. The word 'Noah' carries the promise that through him, God will bring respite and hope amidst human suffering, a theme central to the biblical narrative of redemption.
